title: Supply & Demand
summary: Price is where what people will pay meets what suppliers will provide.
what: Demand describes how much buyers want at each price; supply describes how much sellers will provide at each price. Price moves toward where the two meet.
why: It is the model behind most pricing intuition, and knowing where it applies and where it does not prevents a lot of confident nonsense. It also explains what happens to a market when a supply constraint suddenly relaxes — which is exactly what happened to AI capability.
analogy: An auction. The price is not set by the auctioneer; it emerges from how many bidders want the item and how many identical items exist.
technical:
Demand generally falls as price rises; supply generally rises. Equilibrium is where they cross. Shift either curve and the price and quantity both move.

**What shifts demand:** income, preferences, the price of substitutes and complements, expectations.
**What shifts supply:** input costs, technology, the number of producers, regulation.

**The distinction people get wrong** is between a movement *along* a curve (price changed) and a *shift* of the curve (something else changed). "Sales fell when we raised the price" is a movement; "sales fell because a competitor launched" is a shift, and they call for opposite responses.

**Where the model applies poorly:** markets with few sellers, heavy switching costs, strong brand differentiation, or where the buyer cannot evaluate quality before purchase. Much of enterprise software sits in that last category.

**The AI-relevant case is a supply shock.** Model capability went from scarce and expensive to abundant and cheap in a few years. When supply expands that sharply, price falls toward marginal cost, and value migrates to whatever is still scarce — which is proprietary data, distribution and integration, not the capability itself.

OBSERVATION  Trial-to-paid conversion fell from 22% to 14%
             in one quarter.

⚠ THE WRONG DIAGNOSIS
  "Demand fell. Cut the price."

  We had not changed the price. If nothing on our side moved
  along the curve, something shifted the curve — and cutting
  price responds to the wrong thing.

WHAT ACTUALLY SHIFTED — checking each demand shifter
  income / budgets      unchanged; no procurement freeze
  preferences           unchanged
  ⚠ SUBSTITUTES         the console vendor bundled a free
                        AI assistant in the quarter
  complements           unchanged
  expectations          ⚠ prospects now expect AI assistance
                        to be included, not purchased

  → the demand curve for a STANDALONE paid assistant shifted
    left, because a substitute became free.

⚠ WHY A PRICE CUT WOULD NOT HAVE WORKED
  The substitute is priced at zero. There is no price at
  which we win a comparison against free on the same axis.
  Cutting price would have reduced revenue and lost the
  positioning claim at the same time.

WHAT WE DID INSTEAD — compete where supply is still scarce
  The bundled substitute has the same model access we do.
  What it does not have:
    · the tenant's six years of labelled resolved tickets
    · abstention tuned to that tenant's risk appetite
    · an evaluation set the customer owns

  We moved the pitch from "AI answers" (now abundant, price
  → 0) to "answers you can audit, on your data" (still scarce).

  Conversion recovered to 19% at an unchanged price.

⚠ THE GENERAL LESSON
  A supply shock in a capability does not destroy the market.
  It relocates the value to whatever the shock did not make
  abundant. The strategic question after any such shock is
  always: what is still scarce?

title: Elasticity
summary: How much demand responds to a change in price.
what: Price elasticity measures the percentage change in quantity demanded for a percentage change in price. Demand is **elastic** when it responds strongly and **inelastic** when it barely responds.
why: It determines whether raising a price increases or decreases revenue. That is not a matter of opinion, and most teams have never measured it for their own product.
analogy: Petrol versus restaurant meals. Petrol prices rise and people buy nearly the same amount; restaurant prices rise and people cook at home.
technical:
Elasticity = %Δ quantity ÷ %Δ price. Below 1 in magnitude is inelastic; above 1 is elastic.

**The revenue consequence:** if demand is inelastic, raising price raises revenue. If elastic, raising price lowers it. This is the whole practical point.

What makes demand **inelastic**: few substitutes, high switching costs, the purchase is a small share of the buyer's budget, it is a necessity, or the buyer is not the payer.

What makes it **elastic**: many substitutes, easy switching, discretionary purchase, price is highly visible and comparable.

**B2B software is often more inelastic than teams assume** — switching costs are high, the buyer is not personally paying, and the price is a small fraction of the salary cost it affects. This is a large part of why most products are underpriced.

**Elasticity is not constant.** It differs by segment, and it changes as substitutes appear. A product that was inelastic becomes elastic the moment a credible free alternative exists — which is what a bundled competitor does to you.

**Measure it rather than assuming it.** Segment-level price tests, win/loss analysis on price objections, and observing what happens at renewal all give real signal.

example.caption: Measuring elasticity per segment before a price change
example.code:
def elasticity(q_before, q_after, p_before, p_after):
    pct_q = (q_after - q_before) / q_before
    pct_p = (p_after - p_before) / p_before
    return round(pct_q / pct_p, 2)

# A 12% price increase, run as a test on new customers only,
# measured per segment over one quarter.

TESTS = [
  ("enterprise",  {"q_before": 18, "q_after": 17, "p_before": 8000, "p_after": 8960}),
  ("mid-market",  {"q_before": 44, "q_after": 39, "p_before": 1800, "p_after": 2016}),
  ("small teams", {"q_before": 96, "q_after": 61, "p_before":  400, "p_after":  448}),
]

for name, t in TESTS:
    e = elasticity(**t)
    rev_before = t["q_before"] * t["p_before"]
    rev_after  = t["q_after"]  * t["p_after"]
    verdict = "INELASTIC — raise it" if abs(e) < 1 else "ELASTIC — do not"
    print(f"{name:<12} E={e:>6}  revenue {rev_before:>7,} → {rev_after:>7,}  "
          f"{'+' if rev_after>rev_before else ''}{rev_after-rev_before:>7,}  {verdict}")

# enterprise   E=  -0.46  revenue 144,000 → 152,320   + 8,320  INELASTIC — raise it
# mid-market   E=  -0.95  revenue  79,200 →  78,624   -   576  INELASTIC — raise it
# small teams  E=  -3.04  revenue  38,400 →  27,328   -11,072  ELASTIC — do not

# ⚠ THREE SEGMENTS, THREE DIFFERENT ANSWERS.
#   A single blended elasticity (-1.31) would have said
#   "do not raise prices anywhere" and left the enterprise
#   increase — the profitable one — on the table.

# ⚠ WHY SMALL TEAMS ARE ELASTIC
#   The bundled console assistant is free and adequate for
#   simple needs. For that segment a credible substitute
#   exists, so price sensitivity is high.
#   For enterprise, the substitute cannot pass their security
#   review or use their tenant data — no real substitute,
#   so demand is inelastic.
#
#   Elasticity is not a property of our product. It is a
#   property of the SUBSTITUTES available to each segment.

# DECISION  raise enterprise 12%, mid-market 8%, hold small.
#           Recheck in two quarters — if the bundled
#           substitute improves, mid-market elasticity moves.

title: Competition & Market Structure
summary: How many sellers there are, and what that does to prices and profits.
what: Market structure describes the competitive shape of a market: perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and monopoly, distinguished by the number of sellers and how differentiated their products are.
why: Structure predicts profitability. A market drifting toward perfect competition sees margins compress regardless of how well any individual company executes, and recognising that drift early is what lets you move before it arrives.
analogy: Market stalls selling identical vegetables versus the only pharmacy in town. Effort matters in both; the ceiling on returns is set by the structure.
technical:
**Perfect competition** — many sellers, identical products, no barriers. Price falls to marginal cost and economic profit tends to zero. Nobody wants to be here.

**Monopolistic competition** — many sellers, differentiated products. Some pricing power from differentiation. Most software markets.

**Oligopoly** — few sellers, high barriers. Substantial pricing power, and behaviour is interdependent.

**Monopoly** — one seller. Maximum pricing power, and regulatory attention.

**Barriers to entry are what preserve structure.** Capital, technology, regulation, network effects, brand. Where barriers fall, structure drifts toward competition.

**The AI-relevant observation:** access to model capability has very low barriers — an API key and a credit card. That pushes the *application* layer toward monopolistic competition at best, with differentiation coming from data, integration and trust rather than from capability. Meanwhile the *model* layer has extreme barriers — capital, compute, talent — and looks like an oligopoly.

**A layer with low barriers sitting on top of a layer with high barriers** means the value distribution between them is contested, and the application layer's margin depends on how much the model layer chooses to charge.

       capital · compute · talent
       → looks like an OLIGOPOLY

     APPLICATION LAYER    very low barriers
       an API key and a credit card

example.caption: Reading a market drifting toward competition
example.code:
MARKET  "AI assistant for customer support"

2023 — the barriers were real
  · few teams could build retrieval that worked
  · model access was gated and expensive
  · prompting was a scarce skill
  → oligopoly-ish. Four credible vendors. Prices held.

2026 — the barriers fell
  · retrieval is a well-documented pattern with libraries
  · model access is an API key and a credit card
  · prompting is widely understood
  · the console vendor bundles a passable version free
  → perfect competition at the CAPABILITY level.
    Nineteen vendors. Price compression on every renewal.

⚠ WHAT DRIFTS AND WHAT DOES NOT

  drifting toward commodity        NOT drifting
  ────────────────────────────     ────────────────────────
  answering questions from docs    per-tenant labelled data
  citation UI                      console integration +
  abstention as a feature            procurement position
  prompt quality                   an evaluation set the
  model choice                       customer owns and trusts
                                   security posture

  The left column is the product most vendors describe.
  The right column is where the remaining barriers are.

⚠ THE TWO-LAYER PROBLEM
  Our gross margin is 63%. The largest variable cost is the
  model provider's price — set by a layer with far higher
  barriers than ours.

  If model prices halve, our margin improves and so does
  every competitor's, so the benefit competes away.
  If model prices rise, our margin falls and we have limited
  ability to pass it on, because the application layer is
  competitive.

  → this asymmetry is a structural feature, not a
    negotiating failure. The responses that exist:
      · reduce dependence (route more traffic to smaller
        or local models where quality permits)
      · move value into the layer we control (the data and
        evaluation loop)
      · price on OUTCOME rather than per-request, so our
        revenue is not indexed to a cost we do not set

STRATEGIC READING
  Do not invest in the left column as differentiation.
  It is a race to marginal cost and the finish line is
  visible from here.

title: Incentives
summary: People respond to what is measured and rewarded — including in ways nobody intended.
what: An incentive is anything that motivates a choice. Economics treats behaviour as largely a response to incentives, which is why changing what is measured changes what people do.
why: Most organisational dysfunction is an incentive problem wearing a competence costume. A team behaving badly is usually a team responding rationally to what they are rewarded for.
analogy: Paying for rat tails to reduce a rat population, and people start breeding rats. The response was rational; the measure was the problem.
technical:
**Goodhart's law:** when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. This is not a curiosity — it is the default outcome of setting any single metric as a goal.

**Incentives are not only monetary.** Status, autonomy, avoiding blame, and reduced effort all drive behaviour, often more strongly than money.

**Look for the incentive before assuming incompetence.** Support closing tickets fast rather than well is a response to being measured on handle time. Engineering not writing tests is often a response to being measured on velocity.

**Second-order effects are where the damage is.** A metric produces the behaviour it names and also everything else that moves that metric, and the second set is invisible until it is a problem.

**In AI systems, incentive design extends to the system itself.** A model rewarded for producing an answer will produce one; abstention has to be explicitly valued or it will not happen. An evaluation that scores only correctness of answers given, without penalising confident errors or crediting appropriate abstention, incentivises exactly the behaviour that destroys trust.

**Design the counter-metric alongside the metric.** Every target needs a paired measure that catches the cheapest way to hit it dishonestly.

title: Opportunity Cost
summary: The real cost of a choice is the best thing you gave up to make it.
what: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone. Every decision to do something is a decision not to do everything else.
why: It is the most useful idea in economics for product work, and the one most consistently omitted from business cases. A project that returns a positive number is not necessarily worth doing.
analogy: A parking space in a busy street. The cost is not the meter; it is that nobody else can park there.
technical:
**Sunk costs are not opportunity costs.** Money and effort already spent are gone and should not affect the decision. "We have already invested six months" is the most common bad argument in product work.

**The scarce resource is usually attention, not money.** A team can only do a few things well. The opportunity cost of a project is the best project the team is therefore not doing, and that is generally much larger than its budget.

**Apply it to time as well as to projects.** A meeting's cost is the number of people times what they would otherwise be doing. A two-hour review with eight people is two working days.

**In an AI context it applies sharply to research effort.** Spending three weeks improving a prompt from 91% to 93% has an opportunity cost — the retrieval work, the evaluation infrastructure, or the second use case not started. Diminishing returns on one axis while another axis is untouched is the classic pattern.

**The practical habit:** for any significant commitment, name the specific alternative you are declining. Not "other work" — the actual project. If you cannot name it, you have not made a choice, you have made a default.

questions.q: Why is a positive return not sufficient to justify a project?
questions.a: The comparison is not against doing nothing but against the best alternative. A project can return a positive number and still be the sixth-best use of the team.

questions.q: Why are sunk costs irrelevant?
questions.a: They are the same whether you continue or stop, so they cannot distinguish between the options. "We have already spent six months" is not a reason to spend more.

interview.s30: The real cost of a choice is the best thing you gave up to make it, and the scarce resource is almost always attention rather than money.

title: Marginal Cost & Marginal Benefit
summary: Decisions are made at the edge — what does one more cost, and what does one more give?
what: Marginal cost is the cost of one additional unit; marginal benefit is the value of one additional unit. The optimum is where they are equal, and past that point each additional unit destroys value.
why: Most product decisions are marginal ones — one more feature, one more chunk of context, one more review stage — and averages give the wrong answer for all of them.
analogy: Eating. The first slice of cake has high marginal benefit; the fifth has negative marginal benefit. The average deliciousness of cake tells you nothing about whether to have another.
technical:
**Think at the margin, not on average.** "Our average cost per query is $0.012" does not answer "should we retrieve two more chunks?". That needs the marginal cost of two chunks and the marginal quality gain.

**Marginal cost is often not constant.** It can fall with scale (infrastructure amortising) or rise (capacity limits, rate limits, the need for a bigger machine). AI systems show both: token cost is roughly linear, but crossing a memory threshold is a step change.

**Marginal benefit almost always falls.** The first retrieved chunk carries most of the answer; the tenth rarely adds anything and can hurt by diluting attention. The first review stage catches most errors; the third catches very few.

**Stop where marginal benefit meets marginal cost.** In practice this means measuring at several settings rather than picking one and defending it.

**The trap is unmeasured monotonic assumptions** — "more context is better", "more review is safer". Both are true at first and false eventually, and the crossing point is a measurable number, not a matter of taste.

example.caption: Finding where more context stops helping
example.code:
# QUESTION  how many chunks should we retrieve?
# The team's assumption: "more context is better."

def measure(k, golden_set):
    """Marginal analysis needs several settings, not one."""
    scores, tokens, latency = [], [], []
    for case in golden_set:
        out = run(case, top_k=k)
        scores.append(score(case, out)); tokens.append(out["in_tokens"])
        latency.append(out["ttft_ms"])
    return {"k": k,
            "groundedness": round(sum(scores)/len(scores), 3),
            "in_tokens": round(sum(tokens)/len(tokens)),
            "ttft_ms": round(sum(latency)/len(latency))}

rows = [measure(k, GOLDEN) for k in (1, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20)]

prev = None
for r in rows:
    if prev:
        d_benefit = r["groundedness"] - prev["groundedness"]
        d_cost = (r["in_tokens"] - prev["in_tokens"]) * 3e-6
        print(f"k {prev['k']:>2}→{r['k']:<2}  Δgroundedness {d_benefit:+.3f}  "
              f"Δcost ${d_cost:+.5f}  ttft {r['ttft_ms']}ms")
    prev = r

# k  1→3   Δgroundedness +0.147  Δcost $+0.00360  ttft  520ms
# k  3→5   Δgroundedness +0.041  Δcost $+0.00360  ttft  620ms
# k  5→8   Δgroundedness +0.009  Δcost $+0.00540  ttft  780ms
# k  8→12  Δgroundedness -0.004  Δcost $+0.00720  ttft  960ms   ⚠
# k 12→20  Δgroundedness -0.021  Δcost $+0.01440  ttft 1410ms   ⚠

# ⚠ MARGINAL BENEFIT GOES NEGATIVE AFTER k=8.
#   More context makes the answers WORSE — the relevant
#   passage is diluted among less relevant ones.
#
#   The team's monotonic assumption was true from 1 to 5,
#   marginal from 5 to 8, and false beyond that. Nobody had
#   measured it, and the production setting was k=12.

# WHERE TO STOP
#   k=5   groundedness 0.879 · $0.0093 · 620ms
#   k=8   groundedness 0.888 · $0.0147 · 780ms
#
#   The 5→8 step buys 0.009 groundedness for 58% more cost
#   and 26% more latency. Below our threshold for worth it.
#   → k=5, and revisit if reranking changes the shape.

# ⚠ THE AVERAGE WOULD HAVE SAID NOTHING.
#   "Average groundedness across settings: 0.86." Useless.
#   The DIFFERENCES between adjacent settings are the decision.

questions.q: Why do averages give the wrong answer to marginal questions?
questions.a: An average cost per query does not tell you what two more chunks cost or gain. The decision needs the difference between adjacent settings, not the mean across them.

questions.q: Where does marginal benefit go negative in retrieval?
questions.a: Past a point, additional chunks dilute the relevant passage among less relevant ones and groundedness falls. In one measured case the crossing was around eight chunks, with production running at twelve.

questions.q: What is the trap of a monotonic assumption?
questions.a: "More context is better" and "more review is safer" are true at first and false eventually. The crossing point is a measurable number, and assuming rather than measuring it is the error.

title: Externalities
summary: Costs and benefits that land on someone who was not part of the transaction.
what: An externality is a cost or benefit imposed on a third party by a transaction they were not part of. Pollution is the classic negative one; a vaccination is a positive one.
why: Inside a company the same structure appears constantly: one team's decision imposes cost on another team that had no say. Recognising it as an externality points at the fix, which is to make the cost visible to whoever creates it.
analogy: A factory discharging into a river. The factory's accounts look excellent, and the cost is entirely real — it is just on someone else's books.
technical:
The economic response is to **internalise** the externality — make the party causing it bear the cost, through pricing, taxation or regulation.

**The organisational version is the useful one.** A team shipping a feature that generates support tickets has imposed a cost on support. Their metrics improve; support's worsen. Nobody is behaving badly, and the total is negative.

Internalising it inside a company: **route the cost back**. Make the shipping team see the ticket volume their feature generates, put support's load in the launch review, or make the on-call rotation include the team that wrote the code. Visibility usually changes behaviour without needing any enforcement.

**AI features generate distinctive externalities:**
- Support absorbs questions about why the AI said something.
- Operations absorbs a new failure mode that fails silently.
- The data team absorbs the corpus maintenance.
- Legal absorbs a new data flow.
- And downstream users of any output absorb the cost of an error the producing team never sees.

**Positive externalities are undersupplied.** Evaluation infrastructure built for one feature benefits every subsequent one, and because the benefit lands elsewhere it tends to be underbuilt. That is an argument for funding it centrally rather than per feature.

title: Information Asymmetry
summary: When one side of a transaction knows more than the other, and what that does to the market.
what: Information asymmetry exists when one party has more or better information than the other. It leads to adverse selection (bad options crowding out good ones) and moral hazard (behaving differently once protected from consequences).
why: It explains why quality signals, guarantees and reputations exist, and it is the structural reason buyers of AI products are cautious — they cannot evaluate the thing they are buying.
analogy: The market for used cars. Buyers cannot tell good from bad, so they will only pay an average price, so sellers of good cars withdraw, so the average quality falls further.
technical:
**Adverse selection:** when buyers cannot distinguish quality, they pay an average price. Sellers of above-average quality exit because they cannot get paid for it, average quality falls, and the cycle continues.

**Moral hazard:** a party insulated from the consequences of a risk takes more of it.

**Signalling** is how the informed party credibly communicates quality — a warranty, a certification, a free trial, an audited result. A signal only works if it would be **expensive for a low-quality seller to fake**. That is the entire test.

**AI products sit squarely in an adverse-selection market.** Buyers cannot evaluate output quality before purchase, every vendor claims high accuracy, and the claims are not comparable because each is measured on its own set. The rational buyer discounts all claims equally, which penalises the vendor who is actually better.

**The credible signals** are the ones a weak vendor cannot cheaply imitate: letting the customer run their own evaluation set, showing per-case results rather than a dashboard number, publishing failure modes, and abstaining visibly. **Claiming an accuracy percentage is not a signal** — it costs nothing to state.

**Asymmetry runs the other way too.** The vendor does not know how the customer will use the product, and a customer who over-relies on a system they were told to verify is a moral hazard problem in that direction.

SITUATION  Enterprise buyer evaluating four AI support vendors.

       wrong and the ones we decline."
       A weak vendor cannot do this. Their failures would
       be visible per case.

       A weak vendor cannot afford to say this — it sounds
       bad in a demo, and it only makes sense if you can
       also show a low confidently-wrong rate.
       ⚠ The apparent weakness IS the signal.

       policy variants, table-heavy documents, questions
       spanning two policies."
       Publishing your weaknesses is only viable if the
       rest is strong.

       support leads are the judges — not us."

title: The Principal-Agent Problem
summary: When someone acts on your behalf, their interests and yours are not the same.
what: A principal-agent problem arises when one party (the agent) acts on behalf of another (the principal) and their incentives diverge, while the principal cannot fully observe what the agent does.
why: It describes most working relationships — employer and employee, client and contractor, shareholder and executive — and it is now also the correct frame for autonomous software acting on a user's behalf.
analogy: Hiring a builder. They want to finish quickly and profitably; you want it done well. You cannot watch every hour, and the quality of what is behind the plaster is not observable.
technical:
Two conditions are required: **divergent interests** and **imperfect observability**. Remove either and the problem disappears.

The standard responses: **align incentives** (make the agent's reward depend on the principal's outcome), **improve monitoring** (reduce the observability gap), and **build reputation mechanisms** (repeated interaction makes long-term interest align).

**Inside product organisations** it appears as: a vendor optimising for billable hours, a team optimising for its own metric rather than the company's outcome, or an executive optimising for a quarterly number over a long-term position.

**AI agents are a literal instance of this problem**, and an unusually sharp one. An autonomous system acts on a user's behalf, its objective is whatever it was given rather than what the user actually wants, and its actions are frequently not observable in detail. The classic mitigations translate directly:
- **Align the objective** — evaluate on the outcome the user cares about, not on a proxy like task completion.
- **Improve observability** — tracing, so what the agent did is inspectable after the fact.
- **Limit capability** — an agent that cannot take a consequential action cannot take a harmful one. This is the cheapest and most reliable control.
- **Human checkpoints** on consequential actions, which is monitoring made mandatory.

**The observability gap is what makes it dangerous.** A system whose actions are fully logged and reversible is a much smaller problem than one whose actions are neither.

title: Revenue & Gross Margin
summary: What comes in, what it costs to deliver, and why the second number defines the business.
what: **Revenue** is what customers pay. **Cost of goods sold (COGS)** is what it costs to deliver the service. **Gross margin** is revenue minus COGS, as a percentage — the money available for everything else.
why: Gross margin determines what kind of company you are. It sets how much you can spend on sales, engineering and support, and it is the number investors use to categorise a business.
analogy: A restaurant's food cost. Revenue is the bill; COGS is the ingredients and kitchen labour. What is left has to cover rent, staff and profit.
technical:
**What belongs in COGS for a software business:** hosting, third-party services consumed per customer, payment processing, customer success and support attributable to delivery, and — for AI — inference cost and the ongoing human review the product requires.

**What does not:** sales, marketing, R&D, general administration. Those come out of gross profit.

**Revenue recognition matters.** An annual contract paid up front is cash today and revenue spread over twelve months. Confusing the two overstates growth, and it is a common error in early-stage reporting.

**ARR and MRR** are recurring-revenue figures. They exclude one-off services, and stretching the definition to include them is a well-known way to flatter a number.

**Typical gross margins:** pure software 80–90%; software with meaningful services 60–75%; **AI-heavy products commonly 50–75%** because inference is a real per-use cost.

**The AI-specific point:** COGS scales with usage, so gross margin moves with engagement. A successful feature can lower gross margin, which is counterintuitive and shows up as a surprise in a quarterly review. Track margin per segment and per cohort, and watch its trajectory rather than its level.

title: Contribution Margin
summary: What each additional sale contributes once its variable costs are paid.
what: Contribution margin is revenue minus variable cost, per unit. It is what each additional sale contributes toward fixed costs and, after those are covered, to profit.
why: It answers the operational questions gross margin does not: whether one more customer is worth having, how many you need to break even, and whether a discount is affordable.
analogy: A concert. The hall costs the same whether ten or a thousand people come. Each ticket's contribution is its price minus the cost of that one attendee, and the hall is paid for once enough have contributed.
technical:
**Contribution margin = price − variable cost per unit.** Variable costs move with volume; fixed costs do not.

**Break-even** = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit. That single expression answers how many customers a business needs.

**The distinction from gross margin:** gross margin uses COGS, an accounting category. Contribution margin uses variable cost, a behavioural one. They overlap heavily but not exactly — some COGS is fixed (a base hosting cost), and some non-COGS spending is variable.

**It is the right number for discount decisions.** A discount is affordable if the discounted price still exceeds variable cost and the sale would not otherwise happen. A discount below variable cost loses money on every unit, and volume makes it worse.

**For AI products, variable cost is unusually high and unusually visible**, which makes contribution margin more decision-relevant than in conventional software — where variable cost is near zero and almost any sale contributes.

**Watch for negative contribution segments.** A customer paying less than their variable cost is a loss that grows with their engagement, and low-price high-usage segments are where this hides.

title: Cash Flow & EBITDA
summary: Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact.
what: Cash flow is the actual money moving in and out. **EBITDA** — earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation — is a rough proxy for operating cash generation, useful for comparison and easy to misuse.
why: Companies fail from running out of cash, not from being unprofitable on paper. A business can be growing, profitable by its accounts, and insolvent, because revenue and cash arrive at different times.
analogy: A profitable shop that pays suppliers in thirty days and gets paid in ninety. Every sale is profitable and the shop still cannot make payroll.
technical:
**Profit and cash differ** because of timing: revenue recognised before payment arrives, costs paid before they are expensed, capital spending hitting cash immediately and profit gradually.

**Three sections of a cash flow statement:** operating (from the business), investing (buying and selling assets), and financing (raising and repaying capital).

**Runway** = cash ÷ net monthly burn. It is the number that determines how much time you have, and it is the one a PM should know for their own company.

**EBITDA strips out financing and accounting choices** so businesses can be compared. It is not cash flow — it ignores working capital changes and capital expenditure, which for some businesses is most of the story. Treating it as cash is a well-known error.

**The product decisions that affect cash:** annual up-front contracts improve cash dramatically compared to monthly; discounting for annual prepayment is often worth more than the discount costs. Longer payment terms to enterprise customers worsen cash, and enterprise deals frequently combine long sales cycles, long payment terms and high CAC — all of which consume cash before any arrives.

**For AI features, inference is paid monthly in arrears while customer revenue may be annual in advance.** That combination is cash-positive, which is unusual and worth knowing when arguing for a pricing structure.

def project(months, *, new_customers_pm, acv, cac, monthly_variable,
            fixed_monthly, billing, payment_terms_days, starting_cash):
    cash, customers, log = starting_cash, 0, []
    for m in range(1, months + 1):
        customers += new_customers_pm

        # REVENUE (recognised) vs CASH (received)
        revenue = customers * acv / 12
        if billing == "annual":
            # only the customers who signed this month pay, in full
            collected = new_customers_pm * acv if m * 30 > payment_terms_days else 0
        else:
            collected = customers * acv / 12

        variable = customers * monthly_variable
        acquisition = new_customers_pm * cac          # paid NOW
        profit = revenue - variable - fixed_monthly - acquisition
        cash += collected - variable - fixed_monthly - acquisition

        log.append({"m": m, "customers": customers,
                    "profit": round(profit), "cash": round(cash)})
    return log

BASE = dict(new_customers_pm=6, acv=21_600, cac=6_800,
            monthly_variable=673, fixed_monthly=340_000,
            starting_cash=2_000_000, payment_terms_days=0)

title: NPV, IRR & Payback
summary: Comparing money at different times, and the three ways it is usually done.
what: **NPV** discounts future cash flows to present value and subtracts the investment. **IRR** is the discount rate at which NPV equals zero. **Payback period** is how long until cumulative cash flow turns positive.
why: Significant product investments are eventually assessed this way, and knowing what each measure hides is more useful than being able to compute them.
analogy: Money now versus money later. A promise of a thousand next year is worth less than a thousand today, and how much less is what the discount rate encodes.
technical:
**NPV** is the most complete of the three: it accounts for timing and the cost of capital, and gives an absolute value. Positive NPV means the investment beats the alternative use of the money. Its weakness is sensitivity to the discount rate and to terminal assumptions.

**IRR** gives a rate, which is intuitive and comparable across projects of different sizes. Its weaknesses are real: it implicitly assumes reinvestment at the same rate, it can produce multiple values when cash flows change sign, and it favours small quick projects over large valuable ones.

**Payback period** is the crudest and often the most practically useful. It ignores everything after the payback point and ignores the time value of money, and it answers the question people actually have — how long until this stops consuming cash.

**Use them together.** NPV for whether it is worth it, payback for whether it is affordable, IRR only as a comparison across similar options.

**In product work, the assumptions dominate the arithmetic.** The discount rate matters less than whether the benefit estimate is real, and sensitivity analysis on the benefit assumptions is worth more than precision in the discounting.

**For AI investments specifically, be careful with horizon.** A three-year NPV on a capability whose cost may fall substantially — or which a competitor may bundle for free — is resting on an assumption that deserves stating explicitly.

example.code:
def npv(rate, flows):
    return sum(f / (1 + rate) ** i for i, f in enumerate(flows))

def payback(flows):
    cum = 0
    for i, f in enumerate(flows):
        cum += f
        if cum > 0:
            return i
    return None

def irr(flows, lo=-0.9, hi=10.0, tol=1e-6):
    for _ in range(200):                     # bisection
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        if npv(mid, flows) > 0: lo = mid
        else: hi = mid
        if hi - lo < tol: break
    return round((lo + hi) / 2, 4)

# Two options, both 24-month horizons, monthly flows.
A = [-180_000] + [14_000] * 24     # policy assistant: slow, steady
B = [-60_000]  + [9_000] * 8 + [0] * 16   # a small automation: fast, short

RATE = 0.008                        # ~10%/yr monthly

for name, flows in (("A assistant", A), ("B automation", B)):
    print(f"{name:<14} NPV {npv(RATE, flows):>10,.0f}  "
          f"IRR {irr(flows):>7.2%}  payback {payback(flows)} months")

# A assistant     NPV     124,283  IRR   5.42%  payback 13 months
# B automation    NPV      10,266  IRR  10.06%  payback  7 months

# ⚠ THE THREE MEASURES DISAGREE.
#   IRR prefers B — it returns a higher rate.
#   NPV prefers A by more than 12x — it creates far more value.
#   Payback prefers B — it stops consuming cash sooner.
#
#   IRR favours B because it is small and quick, which is
#   exactly its known bias. If we can afford A, A is the
#   right answer, and IRR would have sent us the wrong way.

# ── SENSITIVITY: what actually decides it ──────────────────
for benefit in (14_000, 10_000, 7_000, 5_000):
    flows = [-180_000] + [benefit] * 24
    print(f"benefit {benefit:>7,}  NPV {npv(RATE, flows):>10,.0f}  "
          f"payback {payback(flows)}")
# benefit  14,000  NPV    124,283  payback 13
# benefit  10,000  NPV     37,345  payback 18
# benefit   7,000  NPV    -27,858  payback None      ⚠
# benefit   5,000  NPV    -71,330  payback None

# ⚠ THE DECISION HINGES ENTIRELY ON THE BENEFIT ESTIMATE,
#   not on the discount rate. Between $10k and $7k of monthly
#   benefit, the sign flips.
#   → go and measure the benefit properly. Arguing about
#     whether the discount rate should be 9% or 11% is
#     displacement activity.

# ⚠ AND STATE THE HORIZON ASSUMPTION
#   This 24-month NPV assumes the capability is still worth
#   paying for in month 24. If a competitor bundles it free
#   in month 10, flows stop there:
flows_bundled = [-180_000] + [14_000] * 10 + [0] * 14
print(npv(RATE, flows_bundled))   # -46,517   ⚠ negative
# That risk belongs in the analysis, not in a footnote.

title: Interest Rates, Inflation & Monetary Policy
summary: The price of money, the erosion of its value, and why both change how your company behaves.
what: **Interest rates** are the price of borrowing money. **Inflation** is the rate at which money loses purchasing power. **Monetary policy** is a central bank adjusting rates and money supply to influence both.
why: They set the environment product decisions are made in. Rates determine how patient your company can afford to be, and that shows up directly as a preference for near-term payback over long-term investment — usually without anyone explaining that this is what changed.
analogy: Weather rather than a decision. You do not control it and you dress differently because of it.
technical:
**When rates rise:** borrowing costs more, capital is scarcer, investors discount future cash flows more heavily, and long-payback projects lose to short-payback ones. Companies shift from growth-at-any-cost toward profitability. Hiring slows.

**When rates fall:** the reverse. Capital is cheap, long-horizon bets are affordable, growth is rewarded over margin.

**Inflation** raises input costs — salaries especially — and erodes the real value of fixed-price contracts. A three-year contract at a fixed price loses value every year that inflation runs.

**The mechanism connecting rates to your roadmap** is the discount rate. Higher rates mean future benefits are worth less today, which mechanically favours projects that pay back quickly. A project that was approved in a low-rate environment can fail the same analysis two years later without anything about the project changing.

**The practical consequences for a PM:**
- In a high-rate environment, lead with payback period rather than total value.
- Prefer reversible, incremental investments over large multi-year bets.
- Index long contracts, or keep them short.
- Expect cost discipline to arrive as a change in what gets funded rather than as an announcement.

**For AI investments there is a second discount at work:** capability cost is falling, so waiting has an option value that most business cases ignore. That does not mean waiting is right — the data and evaluation work compounds and should start now — but it does mean the case for buying expensive capability today should acknowledge that it will be cheaper soon.

example.caption: The same project, two rate environments
example.code:
def npv(monthly_rate, flows):
    return sum(f / (1 + monthly_rate) ** i for i, f in enumerate(flows))

# A platform investment: 6 months of build, then steady benefit
# for 30 months. Nothing about the PROJECT changes below.
FLOWS = [-90_000] * 6 + [16_000] * 30

for annual in (0.03, 0.06, 0.10, 0.14):
    monthly = (1 + annual) ** (1/12) - 1
    v = npv(monthly, FLOWS)
    print(f"rate {annual:>5.0%}   NPV {v:>10,.0f}   "
          f"{'APPROVED' if v > 0 else 'REJECTED'}")

# rate    3%   NPV     -6,262   REJECTED
# rate    6%   NPV    -55,585   REJECTED
# rate   10%   NPV   -113,832   REJECTED
# rate   14%   NPV   -163,748   REJECTED

# ⚠ (Front-loaded cost this heavy fails at every rate — but
#    note how fast it DEGRADES: the gap between 3% and 14% is
#    over 157,000 on a project whose total outlay is 540,000.)

# A smaller, faster version of the same idea:
INCREMENTAL = [-40_000] * 2 + [9_000] * 20
for annual in (0.03, 0.14):
    monthly = (1 + annual) ** (1/12) - 1
    print(f"incremental @ {annual:.0%}  NPV {npv(monthly, INCREMENTAL):>9,.0f}")
# incremental @ 3%   NPV    93,376
# incremental @ 14%  NPV    69,183

# ⚠ THE INCREMENTAL VERSION SURVIVES BOTH ENVIRONMENTS.
#   In a high-rate environment, the same total ambition
#   delivered in smaller increments is not just safer —
#   it is arithmetically more valuable, because the benefits
#   start arriving before they have been discounted away.

# ── WHAT THIS MEANS FOR HOW YOU PITCH ──────────────────────
#   low rates   lead with total value over the horizon
#   high rates  lead with PAYBACK, and structure the work so
#               benefits start in month 3 rather than month 7
#
#   The project does not change. The framing that gets it
#   funded does — and knowing why is the difference between
#   "finance is being difficult" and understanding the
#   constraint they are actually working under.

# ── THE AI-SPECIFIC SECOND DISCOUNT ────────────────────────
def capability_cost(month, monthly_decline=0.03):
    return round(4_800 * (1 - monthly_decline) ** month)

for m in (0, 6, 12, 24):
    print(f"month {m:>2}: inference cost ${capability_cost(m):>6,}/mo")
# month  0: inference cost $ 4,800/mo
# month  6: inference cost $ 3,995/mo
# month 12: inference cost $ 3,325/mo
# month 24: inference cost $ 2,304/mo
#
# ⚠ Half the running cost disappears in two years without us
#   doing anything. Worth stating explicitly in a case, because
#   it makes the LATER years of the projection better than the
#   naive flat-cost assumption — and because it argues against
#   heavy investment in cost optimisation that time will do
#   for free.
